title: Credit Note Template
subtitle: A credit note template for refunds and invoice adjustments — references the original invoice, shows the amount credited, and balances the books. Free download in Excel (auto-calculating), Word, or PDF.
taxHint: Tax from the original invoice applies to the credit
notes: This credit note reduces the amount owed on the original invoice. If the original invoice was already paid, the credit applies to your account or is refunded within 14 days.

Negative amounts entered as negative numbers — the Excel version nets the credit lines automatically
Tax handled correctly — the credit mirrors the tax treatment of the original invoice
Covers every credit scenario — refunds, returned items, pricing corrections and goodwill adjustments

faqs.a: A credit note (also called a credit memo) is a document a business issues to reduce the amount a customer owes on a previous invoice — after a return, a correction, an overcharge or a goodwill discount. It references the original invoice number and shows the amount being credited.

faqs.q: When do I need to issue a credit note?
faqs.a: Whenever you need to lower a previously invoiced amount: returned goods, work not completed, an invoicing error, an overcharge, or a negotiated discount after the invoice was sent. Never edit a sent invoice — issue a credit note against it instead.

faqs.q: Should a credit note show tax?
faqs.a: Generally yes — if sales tax was charged on the original invoice, the credit note reduces the tax as well, mirroring the original taxable lines. That keeps your reported sales tax and your books in sync.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a credit note and a refund?
faqs.a: A credit note is the paperwork; a refund is the money moving. A credit note first reduces the balance on the customer's account. If they had already paid, the credit is then refunded or applied to their next invoice.

overrides.wordBillNote: This Word file works as a ready-made credit note format — the same references, reason field, credited line items and tax treatment as the paper original, but fully editable. Keep one master copy on file and issue a fresh credit note within minutes whenever a bill needs correcting — no need to rebuild the layout every time.
overrides.howToUseText: Use this credit note template whenever you need to reduce the amount a customer owes on an invoice you already sent. Open the file and fill in your business details, then the header fields specific to a credit note: the credit note's own number (continuing your numbering, e.g. CN-0001), the date, the original invoice number being adjusted, and a short reason — returned items, overcharge, work not completed, goodwill. List the amounts being credited on separate lines, mirroring the original invoice's items and tax treatment so your books stay consistent; the Excel version nets the credit lines and the tax automatically to show the total credited. Send it to the customer as a PDF and file it alongside the original invoice — at tax time, credit notes are how you reduce previously reported sales and sales tax rather than silently editing history.

howToUseSteps.title: Reference the original invoice
howToUseSteps.body: Fill in your business details, then the credit note number, date, the original invoice # being adjusted, and the reason — the reference is what ties the two documents together in both your books and the customer's.

howToUseSteps.title: List the credited amounts
howToUseSteps.body: Mirror the original invoice's lines and tax treatment: if tax was charged on an item being credited, the credit line is taxable too. The Excel version nets the lines to a total credited.

howToUseSteps.title: Send it and file it
howToUseSteps.body: Email the credit note as a PDF (Word → Save As → PDF) and file it with the original invoice. If the invoice was already paid, apply the credit to their account or refund within your stated window.

overrides.billingText: The rule that matters most: never edit an invoice after sending it. Once a customer has an invoice, your copy, their copy and any tax you reported all agree on one number — editing it afterward breaks that agreement in ways that surface painfully at audit time. A credit note is the bookkeeping-safe way to correct any of the four situations that generate them: returned goods, work not completed, an overcharge or price error, and goodwill discounts after a complaint. Structure it like a mirror of the original: same line items being credited, same tax treatment, amounts shown as credits, and a header that references the original invoice number and states the reason. Number credit notes in their own sequence (CN-0001, CN-0002…) and store them with the original invoice — together they read as a complete story of what was billed and what was adjusted. On tax: if you collected sales tax on the amount being credited, the credit note should reverse that tax too, which is why the template carries a tax line mirroring the original. If the customer had already paid, the credit becomes either a refund (money out) or account credit (money owed against their next invoice) — say which in the notes. And check whether your state requires credit notes to be issued within a specific window of the original sale for the tax adjustment to count; most departments of revenue publish the rule.
